lead: A program stores values, then acts on them. Operators combine values, control flow decides which statement runs next, strings hold text, and functions name a block so it can be called with different inputs. These four tools turn the constants, types and optionals of the previous chapter into behaviour. Every screen later — a fare label, a login check, a row count — is written with them. Only a few universities teach Swift at this depth, so treat this as working vocabulary for the rest of the unit.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 — the constants, types and optionals being operated on.

blocks.text: Arithmetic is + - * / %. On two Int values, / throws away the remainder: 7 / 2 gives 3. The % operator gives the integer remainder: 7 % 2 gives 1, and the sign follows the left operand, so -7 % 2 gives -1. Write one operand as a Double to keep the fraction: 7.0 / 2.0 gives 3.5.

Comparison operators == != < > <= >= produce a Bool. The single = is assignment, not comparison. The logical operators are && (and), || (or) and ! (not). Swift short-circuits: in a && b, b is skipped when a is false.
A range is written a...b (closed, includes b) or a..<b (half-open, stops before b). 1...5 holds five values, 1..<5 holds four. For an array of count n, loop over 0..<n.
The nil-coalescing operator a ?? b gives a when a is not nil, otherwise b. The ternary condition ? x : y picks x when the condition is true, else y.

if / else if / else runs the first block whose condition is true. guard is the early exit: guard km > 0 else { return "invalid" } leaves the function unless the condition holds, which keeps the main path flat.
switch compares one value against cases. Swift does not fall through — the first match runs and the switch ends. Cases may be ranges and may carry a where clause.

blocks.code:
let km = 12.0
var rate = 0.0
switch km {
case 0...10: rate = 9.0
case 11...: rate = 11.5
default: rate = 11.5
}
print(rate)

blocks.text: A switch must cover every possible value, which is why the default stays.
Loops: for i in 1...5 { } walks a range or a collection; while condition { } tests before each pass; repeat { } while condition runs the body once before testing.

Strings join with + and interpolate with \(...): "Short trip: ₹\(fare)". The properties count and isEmpty, and the methods hasPrefix / hasSuffix, inspect text without changing it. A literal wrapped in triple quotes keeps its line breaks.

func fareLabel(km: Double) -> String declares a function: km is the parameter name, Double its type, String the return type. In func f(label name: Type), label is the argument label typed at the call site and name is the parameter name used inside the body. With one word, as in fareLabel(km: Double), that word is both. Write _ in the label position to drop the label.
A parameter may have a default value. inout lets a function change the caller's variable and is called with &: swap(&a, &b). A function may return a tuple such as (label: String, fare: Double).
A closure is a function you pass around as a value; the table view callbacks in 6.6 are closures.

examples.question: A cab app charges a ₹20 base plus ₹9.0 per km for trips up to 10 km, and ₹11.5 per km beyond that. Write fareLabel(km: Double) -> String and trace it for 8 km and 12 km.
steps: Call 1, km = 8: 8 ≤ 10 is true, rate = ₹9.0. fare = 20 + 8 × 9.0 = 92.0; label "Short trip: ₹92.0".
Call 2, km = 12: 12 ≤ 10 is false, rate = ₹11.5. fare = 20 + 12 × 11.5 = 158.0; label "Long trip: ₹158.0".
examples.check:
def fare(km):
    rate = 9.0 if km <= 10 else 11.5
    return 20 + km * rate
print(fare(8))
print(fare(12))

code.code:
func fareLabel(km: Double) -> String {
    let rate = km <= 10 ? 9.0 : 11.5
    let fare = 20 + km * rate
    let kind = km <= 10 ? "Short" : "Long"
    return "\(kind) trip: ₹\(fare)"
}
print(fareLabel(km: 8))
print(fareLabel(km: 12))

traps: C-style fallthrough: Swift stops at the first match unless fallthrough is written.
Mixing 0...3 (includes 3) with 0..<3 (stops before 3). Looping 0...array.count reads one past the end and crashes.
Integer division: 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. At least one operand must be Double.
Argument label versus parameter name: the label is typed at the call site, and _ removes it.
guard's else must leave the scope with return, break, continue or throw, or the code does not compile.

quiz.a: -1. The sign follows the left operand.

quiz.q: How many values are in the range 1..<5?
quiz.a: Four: 1, 2, 3, 4. The upper bound is excluded.

quiz.q: Why is no break needed at the end of a Swift switch case?
quiz.a: Swift cases do not fall through; the switch ends at the first match. Write fallthrough to continue.

quiz.q: Write the call for func move(by steps: Int, speed s: Double) with 5 steps and speed 2.5.
quiz.a: move(by: 5, speed: 2.5). Outer labels are by and speed; s is used only inside the body.

quiz.q: Trace km = 12 through the switch of this chapter and compute the fare.
quiz.a: 12 matches case 11..., so rate = 11.5; fare = 20 + 12 × 11.5 = 158.0 rupees.

quiz.q: names holds 4 elements. for i in 0...names.count crashes. Why, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: 0...4 gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; index 4 is past the end (valid 0 to 3). Use 0..<names.count or names.indices.

quiz.q: What does a ?? b return when a is nil?
quiz.a: b. When a holds a value, a is returned.

beyond: Not for the exam. async/await, result builders and macros have reshaped how control flow and functions appear in shipping apps, and SwiftUI describes a screen as a function of state. Search 'Swift async await', 'Swift result builder' and 'Swift optional chaining' to go further.
